transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya, Diego, Priya (Redwood); Liam, Sara, Ravi, Asha (ZenithAI)
Recording note: automatic transcript, some mis-hearings expected

Summary (auto): quick runtime profiling deep dive focused on kernel selection tradeoffs, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM results we've seen, and show CUDA graphs to explain where latency is spent. Agreed to run a 48h pilot on 2x H100s and exchange profiling artifacts.

00:00 - Speaker 1 (Maya): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll do a deep dive today, Diego will lead the profiling section. quick intro — Maya from Redwood AE, Diego SE, Priya infra. Liam and team from Zenith?
00:12 - Liam: Yep hi thanks, Liam here. we've been evaluating Redwood for low-latency, high-token-length generation for our agent product. main ask is p95 under 600ms for 2k token continuations but also keep cost per 1k tokens reasonable.
00:25 - Diego: Cool — that's a helpful target. we planned to walk through kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM results we've seen, and show CUDA graphs to explain where latency is spent.
00:38 - Sara: quick note — we are running primarily in our VPC, want to understand private deployment implications and KMS for keying.
00:45 - Maya: noted. Asha will be the network contact on your side?
00:50 - Asha: yes I'll own the network / KMS stuff.
01:02 - Diego: alright jumping in: first slide — workload profile. Zenith said mostly 2k-context chat completions, batch size 1-4, KV cache hit ratio high for multi-turn. tokens per request skewed toward long tails. we tuned kernel selection for common sequence lengths.
01:20 - Diego: one big factor is kernel tiling and the matmul paths. TensorRT-LLM tends to pick fused attention kernels and optimized GEMM for quantized int8 paths. vLLM (we're using latest v0.9 test build) relies on cuBLAS/cuDNN kernels and a custom attention that keeps KV in host or device depending on config.
01:40 - Ravi: can you clarify where the KV cache lives in your tests — device memory or pinned host? we saw spikes when KV spilled to host.
01:48 - Diego: good callout. our baseline for the demo: KV pinned in device memory for H100 with 80GB; we also ran a host-pinned fallback to simulate constrained GPUs. the CUDA graphs show increased PCIe/CPU wake time when KV spills.
02:05 - Priya: small note — our runtime supports automatic prefix caching too. if you have repeated prompts, you'll see p50 improve a lot. p95 is still sensitive to worst-case attention compute.
02:20 - Liam: about quantization — we are experimenting with 4-bit quant for cost. how does kernel selection change for 4-bit vs fp16?
02:28 - Diego: quantization changes both memory footprint and kernel choices. for 4-bit, TensorRT-LLM will pick quantized matmul kernels plus require dequantize/requantize paths for attention scores; vLLM currently falls back more often to fp16 kernels wrapped with quant emulation, so you sometimes lose kernel fusion benefits. result: on long sequences, TRT-LLM 4-bit path gave ~1.6x throughput vs vLLM 4-bit emulation in our 2k tests. caveat: model accuracy varied slightly, need eval pass.
03:00 - Sara: and latency? p95 differences?
03:05 - Diego: p95 was interesting — for batch size 1, TRT-LLM 4-bit p95 was ~720ms for 2k tokens vs vLLM fp16 ~980ms on equivalent hardware. on fp16 TRT-LLM and vLLM were closer, with TRT slightly better due to fused attention kernels.
03:25 - Liam: those numbers are above our 600ms target for 2k. is that end-to-end generation p95 including network and token-streaming?
03:33 - Diego: those are pure inference tail latencies measured on the box, token generation to final token. if you include network RTT and your VPC egress, plan +30-80ms depending on peering. streaming can reduce perceived latency for first tokens.
03:50 - Ravi: can kernel selection be tuned — like force fp16 fused kernels even for quant models?
03:56 - Diego: yes — runtime has a kernel affinity config. we can pin kernel selection policies: prefer_fused, prefer_stable_fp16, prefer_quant. For the pilot we'll run three profiles: prefer_quant, prefer_fused, prefer_fp16 to compare p95 and cost.
04:15 - Maya: Diego, can you show the CUDA graph example you mentioned?
04:20 - Diego: sure — pulling up trace. note the GPU timeline: you can see leaps where attention compute occupies SMs, and small gaps where kernel launch overhead and CPU scheduling adds latency. CUDA graphs reduce these gaps by chaining launches.
04:38 - Diego: in our tests, enabling persistent CUDA graphs for the autoregressive loop removed ~60-120ms of overhead on 2k sequences — that's a big chunk of tail latency. but graphs require predictable loop shapes; variable-length decoding with dynamic stopping can complicate reusing graphs, we use a small set of graphs for buckets (e.g., 128, 512, 1024, 2048).
04:58 - Asha: so variable token lengths — does Redwood do dynamic bucketing?
05:02 - Priya: yes, we do workload-aware bucketing and we also keep a warm graph for the common buckets. for odd lengths we fall back to standard launch which has higher overhead.
05:15 - Sara: are there tradeoffs for memory when you keep multiple graphs resident?
05:21 - Diego: graphs themselves don't take much memory, but the pinned memory and extra frame buffers for precomputation can add a few hundred MB per graph. on H100 80GB it's negligible, on smaller cards it matters.
05:35 - Liam: you mentioned kernel selection differences across vendors — how much variance between H100 vs A100 vs 80GB A40?
05:44 - Diego: H100 has better TFLOPS and different SM scheduling; some fused kernels perform best on H100's sparse/TF32 paths. A100 has stable fp16 paths but kernel latency differs; we saw 10-25% p95 variance depending on kernel. that's why our runtime has a kernel selector that picks the best kernel based on microbenchmarks at startup.
06:05 - Ravi: microbenchmarks — do you run them every deploy? can we pin to a known-good kernel set?
06:10 - Priya: we run a quick microbenchmark on boot and cache the profile. you can also supply a kernel profile artifact if you want to force an exact selection for reproducibility.
06:20 - Liam: about batching — our product is mostly real-time, batch size 1, but with occasional spikes where we could take small batches of 2-4. what's the sweet spot?
06:28 - Diego: for 2k token workloads, batching gives better GPU utilization but increases tail for individual requests. If your p95 SLO matters, prefer batch 1 with CUDA graphs and optimized kernels. If throughput/cost is priority, small batching (2-4) with async routing reduces cost per token. Redwood's smart router can do latency-aware batching: route low-priority requests to batch queues.
06:55 - Liam: is there a predictable cost delta when moving from batch1 to batch4?
07:00 - Diego: depends on model, but roughly 20-35% token-cost reduction moving to batch4 for long sequences due to amortized attention compute.
07:10 - Ravi: curious about quantization at 4-bit — you mentioned accuracy drop. what's the eval process?
07:16 - Diego: we run our Eval harness: 10k example prompts, measure F1/ROUGE or model-specific metrics plus semantic drift tests. For some LLMs 4-bit causes minor regressions on hallucination benchmarks; we flag them. For mission-critical, we recommend fp16 for now.
07:34 - Liam: what about mixed-precision per-layer? can kernel selector do mixed quant/fp16?
07:40 - Diego: yes — we support per-layer precision maps. kernel selection respects layer precision and will pick fused fp16 kernels where precision is fp16 and quant kernels otherwise. This helps keep critical layers in higher precision.
07:55 - Maya: quick pause — any security concerns with TensorRT-LLM binary dependencies on private deployments?
08:00 - Priya: we ship with vetted binaries and provide SBOMs; for Private deployments customers can request audited builds and we support air-gapped installs. KMS integration is supported via customer-managed KMS, we never store plaintext keys.
08:20 - Asha: for VPC peering, we need to know ports and egress. can you send a network checklist?
08:25 - Maya: yes we'll attach the VPC peering checklist in next steps.
08:30 - Diego: back to the profiling: here's a flame view from NVTX. attention kernels dominate ~55% of time, softmax another 10%, kernel launch overhead 12%, KV memcpy (when host spill) 18% — those numbers shift when quantized.
08:48 - Ravi: those memcpy numbers are the killer. is there a config to keep KV strictly on device?
08:52 - Diego: yes — device-only cache policy. downside: max context length limited by device memory. we can do hybrid policies: keep recent turns on device, older history in host with prefetch heuristics.
09:06 - Liam: could prefetching cause jitter in p95?
09:09 - Diego: if prefetch triggers during the critical path, yes. we schedule prefetches during idle gaps or use prewarming. CUDA graphs help schedule these more deterministically.
09:20 - Sara: in terms of observability, can we get token-level latency breakdowns?
09:24 - Priya: yes — Redwood Console exposes token-level timings, per-kernel breakdowns, and NVTX overlays. we'll give you sample dashboards.
09:32 - Diego: also note our runtime exports traces in perfetto/json that you can ingest into your profiler.
09:38 - Liam: great. regarding the pilot — what configs will you run?
09:42 - Diego: plan: three runs — TRT-LLM prefer_quant with CUDA graphs, TRT-LLM prefer_fused fp16 with graphs, and vLLM fp16 baseline. Each run ~24h on 2x H100 with realistic traffic (mix of single-turn and multi-turn). We'll gather p50/p95/p99, memory profiles, and NVTX traces.
09:58 - Ravi: will you simulate our KV cache hit pattern? we'll supply session traces.
10:02 - Diego: yes please send session traces. we'll replay to match your hit ratios.
10:06 - Maya: on costs — we'll also include a compare for per-1k-token cost for these configurations with both on-demand and Dedicated pricing.
10:14 - Asha: about KMS and logs: we need to ensure audit logs don't leak PII. can we redact on the agent?
10:20 - Priya: logs are configurable. you can enable PII scrubbers and we support encryption-at-rest with customer KMS.
10:28 - Liam: any gotchas with CUDA graphs on multi-GPU?
10:31 - Diego: graphs are per-GPU; for multi-GPU pipeline (tensor model parallelism) you need synchronized graphs. we have orchestration to align graphs across GPUs, and we saw good scaling but added complexity for dynamic batching. we'll test that in the pilot.
10:50 - Ravi: how about kernel fallbacks — if a fused kernel fails at runtime, do you automatically switch?
10:55 - Diego: yes — we have a graceful fallback mesh. if the preferred kernel errors or underperforms, runtime switches to cached alternate kernels and reports the event.
11:05 - Sara: SLA questions — if we run Dedicated, what's the expected uptime for these heavy profiles?
11:10 - Maya: Dedicated has SLA commitments; we'll share the SLA doc. practically, we aim for <1% error/retry overhead and will set up canary deployments.
11:20 - Liam: last technical question — are there reproducibility options for exact kernel selection and seed?
11:24 - Priya: we can fix the kernel profile, disable auto-tuning, and fix RNG seeds for deterministic outputs. some non-determinism remains in optimized kernels but it's small.
11:35 - Diego: ok wrapping up — immediate next steps: Diego will run the three config profiles and share results; Maya will send pricing and VPC checklist; Ravi to send session traces; Asha to confirm KMS/network details.
11:50 - Maya: thanks everyone. we'll target follow-up next week to review pilot results.
11:58 - Liam: thanks, appreciate the deep dive.
12:05 - (call end)
